title: Developmental malformation of the corpus callosum: a review of typical callosal development and examples of developmental disorders with callosal involvement

subsections.section_title: Typical Corpus Callosum Development and Structure
subsections.subsection_title: Embryological and Fetal Development of the Corpus Callosum
subsections.content:
The embryological development of the corpus callosum begins in the human fetus around the 8th to 10th week of gestation, when callosal axons from the cingulate cortex begin to cross the midline through a specialized glial-rich structure known as the glial wedge and indusium griseum. This process is preceded by the infolding of the dorsal lamina reuniens of His, forming a median groove that fuses to create the massa commissuralis, which serves as the foundational scaffold for the corpus callosum ref [2]. By the 12th week, pioneering axons establish the initial callosal pathway, guided by molecular cues such as Slit, Netrin, and Semaphorin3A, which are conserved between rodents and humans ref [3]. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies of fixed fetal brains between 13 and 20 weeks of gestation have enabled visualization of the corpus callosum’s early formation alongside other commissures, confirming the presence of homologous midline glial populations to those in mouse models ref [3].

Between 18 and 20 postconceptual weeks, the corpus callosum undergoes rapid growth mediated by transient laminar and modular structures, including the subcallosal zone and callosal septa, which provide structural and molecular guidance for axonal extension along the ventral tier ref [4]. These structures, rich in glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-positive cells and extracellular matrix components such as chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, facilitate the progressive thickening of the callosal midsagittal cross-section ref [4]. By the second trimester, DTI tractography reveals the emergence of distinct callosal fiber bundles, with the genu forming before the splenium, reflecting a rostrocaudal gradient of maturation ref [1]. The cavum septi pellucidum, initially open to the interhemispheric fissure, becomes sealed by the rostrum of the corpus callosum in humans, a feature distinguishing primates from lower mammals ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Typical Corpus Callosum Development and Structure
subsections.subsection_title: Functional Correlates of Callosal Integrity
subsections.content:
The integrity of the corpus callosum is critically linked to the efficiency of interhemispheric communication, with microstructural properties directly influencing behavioral performance. Diffusion tensor imaging studies have demonstrated that fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (D) in the corpus callosum correlate with the speed and accuracy of interhemispheric transfer, particularly in visuomotor tasks. For instance, reduced FA and elevated diffusivity in the genu and splenium are associated with prolonged crossed-uncrossed differences (CUD) in reaction time tasks, indicating impaired transfer of sensory and motor information between hemispheres ref [6]. Similarly, white matter integrity in the body of the corpus callosum predicts bimanual coordination skills, with probabilistic tractography linking this region to the supplementary and cingulate motor areas ref [5].

Beyond motor functions, callosal microstructure also supports higher-order cognitive processes. In children, diffusivity perpendicular to temporal callosal fibers correlates positively with phonological awareness, suggesting that efficient interhemispheric connectivity in auditory-language networks underpins reading acquisition ref [7]. These findings align with evidence that the corpus callosum facilitates both excitatory integration and inhibitory suppression across hemispheres, enabling functional lateralization and reducing interhemispheric interference ref [9]. Behavioral studies using lateralized visual stimuli further reveal that even in intact brains, subtle interhemispheric transfer latencies exist, modulated by stimulus properties and callosal integrity, with acallosal individuals exhibiting intermediate CUDs attributable to alternative subcortical pathways ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Typical Corpus Callosum Development and Structure
subsections.subsection_title: Topographical Organization and Fiber Composition
subsections.content:
The topographical organization of the corpus callosum reflects a systematic somatotopic and functional mapping of interhemispheric connections, with distinct fiber bundles projecting to specific cortical regions. Early work by Witelson proposed a five-partition scheme based on primate data, but modern diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography has refined this model in humans, revealing that motor fibers terminate more posteriorly than previously assumed, particularly within the posterior body and isthmus ref [10]. Subsequent parcellation studies using DTI have identified six major subdivisions of the corpus callosum, each corresponding to projections from prefrontal, premotor, primary motor, primary sensory, parietal, and occipitotemporal cortices ref [11]. Notably, motor fibers exhibit somatotopic organization, with hand-related projections located anteriorly and ventrally relative to foot-related fibers, and their microstructural integrity (as measured by fractional anisotropy) correlates with functional interhemispheric inhibition ref [12]. Occipital callosal fibers, critical for visual integration, converge in the splenium and are organized by visual field maps: dorsal stream projections (V3, V3A, V7) occupy the central splenium, while ventral stream fibers (V4) terminate in its inferior-anterior region ref [7]. Cortical lesion studies corroborate this organization, showing that lesions in inferior frontal and temporo-parieto-occipital regions produce Wallerian degeneration in the genu and splenium, respectively, with no degeneration observed after anterior superior frontal lesions ref [14].

These findings collectively demonstrate that the corpus callosum is not a homogeneous structure but a highly organized conduit with precise topographical fidelity, where fiber composition and spatial arrangement directly reflect the functional architecture of the connected cortical areas.

subsections.section_title: Typical Corpus Callosum Development and Structure
subsections.subsection_title: Microstructural Maturation from Childhood to Adulthood
subsections.content:
The microstructural maturation of the corpus callosum (CC) from childhood to adulthood is characterized by progressive increases in axonal packing, myelination, and fiber organization, as revealed by diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Longitudinal MRI studies demonstrate a non-linear increase in CC area, particularly in the splenium, with the most robust growth occurring during early childhood and adolescence, plateauing by late teens ref [5]. DTI metrics such as fractional anisotropy (FA) rise and mean diffusivity (MD) decline across the CC, reflecting enhanced microstructural integrity, with regional heterogeneity indicating delayed maturation in fronto-temporal connections compared to posterior regions ref [16]. These changes correlate with improved interhemispheric transfer efficiency, as evidenced by decreasing evoked potential transmission times and increasing bilateral field advantages during development ref [6]. In adolescents, higher FA in the splenium and body of the CC is associated with superior visuospatial, psychomotor, and language performance, underscoring the functional relevance of callosal microstructure ref [7]. The protracted maturation of the CC extends into the third decade of life, aligning with the protracted development of higher-order cognitive networks and executive functions.

Regional variations in maturation timing suggest a caudal-to-rostral gradient, with the splenium maturing earlier than the genu, consistent with the hierarchical development of sensory and motor versus prefrontal integration systems. This pattern is mirrored in white matter tracts throughout the brain, where association fibers mature later than projection fibers ref [16]. The protracted development of the CC underscores its role in supporting the increasing complexity of interhemispheric communication required for advanced cognitive functions during adolescence and early adulthood.

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroplasticity and Structural Adaptations in Callosal Dysgenesis
subsections.content:
In cases of callosal dysgenesis, the developing brain exhibits remarkable neuroplasticity by rerouting interhemispheric connections through alternative pathways when the corpus callosum fails to form properly. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies have revealed that, despite the absence or severe hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, residual callosal fibers maintain a topographical organization similar to that of typical development, preserving connections between homotopic cortical regions ref [19]. Notably, two aberrant tracts consistently emerge: the Probst bundle, which runs parallel to the midline within each hemisphere, and a previously undocumented sigmoidal bundle that connects the frontal lobe with the contralateral occipitoparietal cortex, demonstrating heterotopic but functionally significant rewiring ref [19]. These adaptations suggest that axonal guidance mechanisms retain some developmental precision even in the absence of midline crossing cues, with fiber topography preserved despite gross structural anomalies ref [19].

Comparative studies using in vivo DTI have shown that the topographical organization of the corpus callosum in humans closely mirrors that of nonhuman primates, particularly in the caudal extension of frontal fibers, implying conserved developmental constraints that may guide compensatory wiring in dysgenesis ref [7]. Revisions to Witelson’s classical model, informed by high-resolution tractography, further clarify the cortical mapping of callosal fibers, providing a framework to interpret aberrant projections in dysgenetic brains ref [14]. These structural adaptations may underlie preserved interhemispheric communication in some individuals, as suggested by behavioral studies indicating that functional integration between hemispheres can be maintained through subcortical and anterior commissural pathways, even without a fully formed corpus callosum ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Syndromes with Callosal Agenesis or Hypoplasia
subsections.content:
Callosal agenesis or hypoplasia is a recognized neuroanatomical feature in several genetic syndromes, with Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaic variants) representing one of the most consistently documented associations. Cases of agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) have been reported in patients with 45,X karyotype, as well as in mosaic forms such as 45,X/48,X,r(X), often co-occurring with distinctive somatic features including kabuki-like facies, renal anomalies, and thyroid autoimmunity ref [22], ref [23], ref [25]. These reports suggest that X-chromosome monosomy may disrupt midline brain development, though the penetrance remains low and the pathogenic mechanism incompletely understood. Beyond Turner syndrome, chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) is increasingly recognized for its association with callosal abnormalities, though typically manifesting as hypoplasia or morphological distortion rather than complete agenesis. Structural MRI studies reveal enlarged rostrum and isthmus regions, altered callosal curvature, and reduced age-related growth trajectories in children with 22q11DS ref [9], ref [15]. Diffusion tensor imaging further demonstrates microstructural white matter alterations in interhemispheric tracts, implicating disrupted axonal organization in the corpus callosum ref [17]. These findings highlight that callosal malformations in 22q11DS are not merely secondary to ventricular enlargement but reflect primary developmental dysgenesis.

The phenotypic spectrum of callosal anomalies in these syndromes underscores the role of specific genomic regions in midline patterning. While ACC in Turner syndrome is rare and often accompanied by multisystem anomalies, callosal dysmorphology in 22q11DS is more prevalent and correlates with cognitive and psychiatric risk profiles, including increased schizotypy. The convergence of structural and microstructural abnormalities across these distinct genetic conditions emphasizes the corpus callosum as a sensitive target of developmental disruption in chromosomal disorders.

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Clinical Diagnosis of Callosal Malformations
subsections.content:
Callosal malformations, including agenesis (ACC) and hypoplasia (HCC), occur in approximately 1.8 per 10,000 live births, as demonstrated in a large population-based study from California spanning 1983–2003, with a male predominance (52%) and a strong association with prematurity (relative risk 3.7 for births <37 weeks gestation) ref [28]. Advanced maternal age (≥40 years) significantly increases risk, particularly in cases with concurrent chromosomal abnormalities, where the relative risk for ACC reaches 5.9 ref [28]. These anomalies are rarely isolated; up to 49.5% of cases involve additional CNS malformations, and comorbidities such as cardiac (27.6%) and musculoskeletal (33.5%) defects are common, underscoring their role as markers of multisystem developmental disruption ref [28].

Prenatal diagnosis has become increasingly critical, with fetal MRI now the gold standard for detecting ACC and distinguishing complete from partial forms, the latter often underdiagnosed due to technical limitations ref [29]. Complete ACC is associated with significantly worse neurodevelopmental outcomes compared to partial ACC (p = 0.001), especially when accompanied by other structural anomalies (p < 0.01) ref [29]. Detailed fetal anatomical surveys and karyotyping are essential for accurate prognostication and parental counseling ref [29]. MRI also plays a pivotal role in diagnosing callosal anomalies within neurocutaneous syndromes, such as tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis type 1, where characteristic cortical and subependymal lesions can co-occur with callosal dysgenesis, enabling integrated diagnostic assessment ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Congenital and Genetic Disorders with Callosal Involvement
subsections.subsection_title: Neurocognitive and Behavioral Phenotypes in Callosal Agenesis
subsections.content:
Individuals with agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) often exhibit distinct neurocognitive and behavioral phenotypes, even in the absence of intellectual disability. Social cognition is notably impaired, with deficits in interpreting emotional cues, inferring mental states, and generating coherent social narratives, as demonstrated through Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) analyses showing reduced use of emotion- and social-process-related language ref [18]. These deficits extend to difficulties in recognizing and verbalizing emotions, a trait linked to alexithymia, which may arise from disrupted interhemispheric transfer of affective information, particularly from the right to left hemisphere ref [14]. Parent-reported data using the Child Behavior Checklist reveal elevated rates of attentional problems, social withdrawal, and unusual thoughts in older children with ACC, though typically less severe than in autism spectrum disorder ref [32]. Despite normal IQ, individuals with ACC show impaired executive function, reduced cognitive flexibility, and difficulties with abstract reasoning and complex problem-solving ref [20].

Neurobehavioral outcomes are heterogeneous, with some individuals presenting with mild impairments while others exhibit significant psychosocial challenges. Linguistic analyses of TAT narratives indicate a tendency toward present-tense, self-referential speech, suggesting a diminished capacity for imaginative projection into others' perspectives ref [18]. The absence of classic disconnection syndromes seen in acquired callosal lesions underscores the brain’s compensatory plasticity, yet functional deficits persist in tasks requiring interhemispheric integration, particularly those involving complex social or emotional stimuli ref [36]. Clinical studies report that approximately 30% of children with ACC have normal or mildly delayed development, but the majority show moderate to severe impairments, often co-occurring with epilepsy, microcephaly, or dysmorphic features ref [12]. These findings highlight ACC as a disorder of distributed neural networks rather than isolated structural absence, with behavioral phenotypes shaped by both primary callosal absence and secondary compensatory mechanisms.

subsections.section_title: Acquired and Prenatal Influences on Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Prenatal Alcohol Exposure and Callosal Malformations
subsections.content:
Prenatal alcohol exposure is a well-documented teratogen associated with structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum (CC), particularly in fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). Early autopsy studies first identified CC agenesis in severe cases, a finding later corroborated in vivo using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which revealed not only complete agenesis but also significant reductions in CC area across multiple regions in exposed children compared to controls ref [39]. Quantitative MRI analyses have since demonstrated that posterior CC regions—including the isthmus and splenium—are disproportionately affected, suggesting regional vulnerability to alcohol-induced disruption during mid-to-late gestation ref [7]. These microstructural anomalies are further confirmed by diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), which shows reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) and increased mean diffusivity (MD) in posterior callosal tracts, indicative of impaired myelination and axonal organization ref [41], ref [6], ref [7].

Functional consequences of these structural deficits are evident in impaired interhemispheric communication, particularly in tasks requiring bimanual coordination without visual feedback, where children with FASD exhibit reduced accuracy and increased variability ref [41]. Notably, visuomotor integration deficits correlate specifically with splenial FA reductions, highlighting the functional relevance of posterior CC integrity in FASD ref [6]. While anterior regions such as the genu show less consistent involvement, trends toward reduced FA in this area suggest a gradient of vulnerability along the CC’s anterior-posterior axis ref [7]. Collectively, these findings underscore the CC as a primary target of alcohol’s neuroteratogenic effects, with structural and microstructural alterations contributing to the neurobehavioral phenotype of FASD ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Acquired and Prenatal Influences on Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Corpus Callosum Integrity in Developmental Language Disorders
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence suggests that corpus callosum (CC) integrity may be compromised in children with developmental language disorders (DLD), though findings remain heterogeneous. Early morphometric studies reported no significant differences in total CC area between children with phonologic-syntactic DLD and typically developing controls when corrected for forebrain volume, suggesting that gross callosal size may not be a primary anatomical marker of DLD ref [42]. However, functional assessments reveal more nuanced deficits: children with DLD exhibit impaired interhemispheric transfer of tactile information, as evidenced by significantly higher error rates in crossed-hand localization tasks compared to age-matched controls, implicating callosal dysfunction in sensory-motor integration underlying language processing ref [43]. Furthermore, neuroanatomical risk indices derived from brain asymmetry and volume patterns predict distinct language profiles, with reduced structural symmetry correlating with severe receptive language impairments characteristic of DLD, pointing to a broader neurodevelopmental architecture that includes callosal connectivity ref [44].

Recent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies extend these findings by linking microstructural alterations in specific callosal tracts—particularly those connecting temporal and frontal language regions—to phonological and syntactic deficits. For instance, reduced fractional anisotropy in the posterior CC has been associated with impaired phonological processing, suggesting that disrupted white matter integrity, rather than mere size, may underlie core language impairments in DLD. These microstructural anomalies may reflect delayed myelination or aberrant axonal organization, consistent with the protracted maturation of the CC into adolescence. Collectively, these data support a model in which DLD involves not only cortical language networks but also compromised interhemispheric communication via the corpus callosum, highlighting its role as a critical substrate for integrated language function.

subsections.section_title: Acquired and Prenatal Influences on Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: White Matter Microstructure and Functional Consequences
subsections.content:
The microstructural integrity of white matter, particularly in the corpus callosum, plays a critical role in interhemispheric communication and higher-order cognitive functions. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies in newborns have established normative trajectories of diffusion anisotropy and apparent diffusion coefficient, revealing that callosal maturation follows a caudal-to-rostral gradient, with later-myelinating regions showing progressive increases in fractional anisotropy and reduced radial diffusivity ref [46]. These microstructural changes correlate with the emergence of bimanual coordination, language processing, and executive function. In developmental language disorder (DLD) and autism, white matter volume increases are localized to the radiate compartment, suggesting a postnatal disruption in myelination or axonal organization that preferentially affects corticocortical connections rather than deep or callosal fibers ref [5]. Such anomalies are associated with reduced interhemispheric transfer efficiency, as evidenced by prolonged evoked potential latencies and impaired performance on tasks requiring rapid interhemispheric integration. Moreover, microstructural alterations in the corpus callosum—particularly in the splenium and genu—are linked to deficits in phonological processing and semantic fluency, underscoring the functional consequences of disrupted white matter architecture.

Beyond DLD and autism, prenatal insults such as alcohol exposure and preterm birth further compromise callosal microstructure, with DTI revealing reduced fractional anisotropy and increased mean diffusivity in these populations. These changes are not merely structural but are predictive of long-term neurobehavioral outcomes, including attentional deficits and language delays. The convergence of microstructural abnormalities across diverse neurodevelopmental conditions highlights the corpus callosum as a sensitive biomarker of disrupted white matter development and a key substrate for functional impairments in interhemispheric integration.

subsections.section_title: Acquired and Prenatal Influences on Callosal Development
subsections.subsection_title: Preterm Birth and Corpus Callosum Development
subsections.content:
Preterm birth is associated with significant disruptions in the development of the corpus callosum (CC), particularly affecting its posterior regions and microstructural integrity. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies reveal that preterm infants exhibit reduced fractional anisotropy and elevated radial diffusivity in the splenium and posterior limb of the internal capsule, indicating impaired myelination and axonal organization at term-equivalent age ref [10]. These microstructural alterations persist into childhood, with longitudinal studies demonstrating smaller CC volumes in adolescents born very preterm, especially in the mid-posterior and posterior quarters, even after adjusting for total white matter volume ref [50]. The growth trajectory of the CC is also compromised, with serial cranial ultrasound measurements showing a marked slowing in CC length gain after the first two weeks of life in very low birthweight infants, detectable as early as 6 weeks postnatally ref [12].

These structural deficits correlate with functional outcomes: reduced CC size is associated with poorer motor performance, as evidenced by inverse relationships between CC area and motor impairment scores in preterm children at 7–8 years of age ref [6]. In boys, smaller CC dimensions are specifically linked to deficits in verbal fluency and verbal IQ, suggesting sex-specific vulnerabilities in language-related interhemispheric communication ref [50]. Furthermore, children born preterm without focal brain injury still demonstrate regionally specific white matter microstructural abnormalities that correlate with lower developmental quotients in motor, language, and coordination domains, highlighting the sensitivity of the CC to prematurity-related stressors ref [11]. Perinatal complications such as periventricular hemorrhage and ventricular dilatation exacerbate CC thinning, underscoring the role of neonatal morbidity in callosal maldevelopment ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders with Callosal Abnormalities
subsections.subsection_title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Corpus Callosum Morphometry
subsections.content:
Structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum (CC) in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have been consistently documented, with meta-analytic evidence revealing region-specific reductions in callosal size. A comprehensive meta-analysis of 13 studies found that children and adolescents with ADHD exhibit a smaller splenium compared to typically developing peers, an effect primarily driven by females with ADHD, while males showed reduced rostral body volume, suggesting sex-specific neuroanatomical profiles ref [52]. These morphometric differences may reflect disrupted interhemispheric integration, particularly in motor and attentional networks. In children with neurofibromatosis-1 and comorbid ADHD, total CC area was enlarged relative to controls, yet no significant difference was observed between those with and without ADHD, indicating that ADHD symptoms in this genetic subgroup may arise from neurochemical rather than gross structural alterations ref [53].

Functional studies using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) have further implicated callosal dysfunction in ADHD. Children with ADHD demonstrate prolonged latency and shortened duration of the ipsilateral silent period (iSP), a measure of transcallosal motor inhibition, suggesting impaired myelination or synaptic efficiency within callosal fibers ref [54]. These deficits are not static: treatment with methylphenidate significantly prolongs iSP duration and reduces latency, correlating with clinical symptom improvement, thereby implicating callosal inhibition as a modifiable neurophysiological target ref [55]. Additionally, deficient intracortical inhibition in drug-naive ADHD children is normalized by methylphenidate, pointing to a broader cortical disinhibition that may involve callosal circuitry ref [19]. The association between cortical disinhibition and ADHD symptom severity, independent of tics in Tourette syndrome, further supports a direct link between inhibitory control deficits and callosal-mediated network dysfunction ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders with Callosal Abnormalities
subsections.subsection_title: Callosal Morphology and Dyslexia: Structural and Functional Links
subsections.content:
Structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum in dyslexia have been consistently linked to atypical interhemispheric communication, particularly in posterior regions supporting language processing. Early MRI studies revealed that dyslexic adults exhibit a significantly larger splenium and posterior third of the corpus callosum compared to typical readers, suggesting compensatory or anomalous connectivity between right and left temporoparietal cortices ref [58]. This enlargement, observed in both male and female dyslexic individuals, may reflect reduced lateralization of language functions and increased reliance on bilateral processing ref [59]. Subsequent research using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) has refined this view, demonstrating that reduced perpendicular diffusivity in the temporal-callosal pathway—indicative of more organized or myelinated axons—is associated with superior phonological skills, implying that efficient, rather than merely increased, interhemispheric connectivity underpins reading proficiency ref [7].

Functional studies further support this model, showing that phonologically dyslexic adults exhibit impaired transcallosal transfer of tactile and motor information, particularly during complex bimanual tasks requiring interhemispheric integration ref [6]. These deficits correlate with phonological processing scores, suggesting that the corpus callosum mediates not only structural but also dynamic aspects of reading-related neural coordination. Family-based MRI analyses have confirmed that within-family variation in oral reading ability is associated with midbody callosal area, independent of IQ and brain volume, reinforcing the heritable neuroanatomical basis of dyslexia ref [60]. Together, these findings indicate that dyslexia involves a complex interplay between callosal morphology and microstructural integrity, where both overconnectivity in posterior regions and underconnectivity in specific pathways may disrupt the precise timing and lateralization required for fluent reading.

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders with Callosal Abnormalities
subsections.subsection_title: Corpus Callosum Abnormalities in Autism Spectrum Disorder
subsections.content:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is consistently associated with structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum (CC), particularly reductions in size that reflect altered interhemispheric connectivity. Early MRI studies reported decreased CC area in ASD, with the most pronounced deficits localized to the posterior regions, including the splenium, which contains fibers connecting parietal and occipital cortices ref [11]. Subsequent research confirmed these findings across diverse cohorts, including both high-functioning individuals and those with co-occurring intellectual disability, indicating that CC hypoplasia is not confined to a specific cognitive subgroup ref [65]. More recent analyses using high-resolution morphometry and three-dimensional mapping have revealed that callosal reductions extend beyond the posterior third, with significant thinning also observed in the genu and midbody, suggesting widespread disruption of cortical connectivity ref [67].

Notably, CC size in ASD must be interpreted relative to overall brain volume, as many individuals with ASD exhibit macrocephaly and increased total brain size. Studies controlling for head size demonstrate that the CC is disproportionately small in ASD, even when absolute dimensions appear normal, pointing to a specific deficit in interhemispheric white matter organization rather than generalized growth alterations ref [8]. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) further reveals microstructural abnormalities, including reduced fractional anisotropy and elevated radial diffusivity in the CC, particularly in a subgroup of individuals with lower performance IQ, implicating myelin integrity in functional impairments ref [9]. Regional analyses across developmental stages indicate that callosal deficits are detectable in early childhood and persist into adolescence, supporting a neurodevelopmental origin ref [62]. These findings collectively position CC abnormalities as a key neuroanatomical marker of aberrant cortical connectivity in ASD.

subsections.section_title: Supplementary Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Callosal Agenesis in Genetic Syndromes
subsections.content:
Agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) is a rare but documented neuroanatomical anomaly in several genetic syndromes, particularly those involving sex chromosome abnormalities. Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaic variants) has been associated with ACC in multiple case reports, suggesting a potential link between X-chromosome monosomy and disrupted midline brain development. Early reports documented ACC in patients with 45,X karyotypes, often accompanied by cognitive deficits and somatic features such as horseshoe kidney and Hashimoto's thyroiditis ref [23], ref [24]. More recently, a case of 45,X/48,X,r(X) mosaicism presented with ACC alongside distinctive Kabuki-like facial features, indicating that ring X chromosomes may confer a higher risk of CNS malformations than previously recognized ref [22].

Morphometric studies further reveal that even in the absence of complete ACC, Turner syndrome is associated with significant callosal reductions, particularly in the genu, as well as cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, suggesting a broader pattern of midline structural vulnerability ref [26]. Similarly, chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) demonstrates a high prevalence of callosal dysgenesis, with studies reporting both increased total callosal area and altered growth trajectories in nonpsychotic children, pointing to aberrant developmental patterning rather than simple atrophy ref [19]. In Williams syndrome, caused by a 7q11.23 deletion, the corpus callosum is consistently smaller, with pronounced reductions in the splenium and caudal body, alongside increased voxel intensity suggesting altered myelination or water content ref [20]. These findings underscore that ACC and callosal dysmorphology are not isolated anomalies but integral components of distinct neurogenetic phenotypes, reflecting the sensitivity of callosal development to specific gene dosage effects.

subsections.section_title: Supplementary Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Prenatal Insults and Callosal Development
subsections.content:
Prenatal insults significantly disrupt the normal development of the corpus callosum, with evidence pointing to structural alterations following exposure to prematurity, alcohol, and other teratogenic agents. Very preterm birth, particularly before 33 weeks' gestation, is consistently associated with reduced corpus callosum volume, especially in the posterior and mid-posterior regions, as demonstrated by MRI studies in adolescents and children ref [47]. These reductions correlate with impaired neuropsychological outcomes, including diminished verbal fluency and IQ, particularly in preterm boys ref [47]. Similarly, motor performance deficits in preterm children without cerebral palsy are strongly linked to smaller total and regional callosal areas, suggesting that even subclinical callosal underdevelopment affects motor integration ref [48]. Prenatal alcohol exposure represents another major insult, with studies revealing both complete agenesis and selective thinning of callosal subregions in children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, even after correcting for total brain size ref [37]. Microstructural abnormalities, including reduced fractional anisotropy and altered white matter integrity, further underscore the vulnerability of callosal axons to in utero toxicants ref [4]. These findings highlight the corpus callosum as a sensitive target of prenatal disruption, with region-specific vulnerabilities that manifest in distinct neurobehavioral phenotypes across the lifespan.

The timing and nature of the insult appear to dictate the pattern of callosal malformation: early insults (e.g., periventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants) predominantly affect posterior callosal segments, while chronic teratogenic exposure (e.g., alcohol) may produce more diffuse or regionally selective atrophy. The posterior corpus callosum, which integrates sensory and higher-order cognitive information, is particularly susceptible, potentially explaining the frequent co-occurrence of visuospatial, language, and motor deficits in affected populations. Longitudinal data suggest that these structural anomalies persist into adolescence and adulthood, implicating early developmental disruption rather than secondary degeneration as the primary mechanism ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Supplementary Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Callosal Abnormalities in Williams Syndrome and 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
subsections.content:
Williams syndrome (WS), caused by a hemizygous deletion at 7q11.23, is associated with distinct corpus callosum (CC) morphological alterations. Studies using high-resolution MRI reveal a reduced total midsagittal CC area, with disproportionate thinning of the splenium and isthmus—regions connecting parieto-occipital cortices—consistent with the characteristic visuospatial deficits in WS ref [27]. Geometrical modeling further demonstrates an increased bending angle of the CC and altered thickness profiles, particularly in posterior segments, suggesting aberrant white matter organization ref [71]. Notably, the enlarged ventral anterior prefrontal cortex in WS correlates with the CC bending angle, implicating a structural network underlying the syndrome’s atypical social communication profile ref [70].

In contrast, 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) exhibits widespread white matter microstructural disruptions, including reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) in interhemispheric tracts, particularly within the CC, as revealed by diffusion tensor imaging ref [6]. These microstructural deficits are not uniformly distributed but are most pronounced in frontal and brainstem-connected callosal regions, potentially contributing to the high risk of psychosis and cognitive impairments in 22q11DS. While CC volume reductions have been reported, the primary pathology appears to lie in axonal integrity and myelination rather than gross size ref [6]. Together, these findings highlight that despite both being microdeletion syndromes, WS and 22q11DS manifest divergent callosal phenotypes: WS shows regionally selective atrophy linked to behavioral strengths and weaknesses, whereas 22q11DS presents with diffuse microstructural disorganization reflecting broader white matter vulnerability.

subsections.section_title: Supplementary Materials
subsections.subsection_title: Corpus Callosum Morphology in Autism Spectrum Disorder
subsections.content:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is consistently associated with altered corpus callosum (CC) morphology, particularly in regional substructures. Early magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies revealed a reduced size of the posterior CC in individuals with ASD, with the most pronounced deficits observed in the midbody and splenium, regions rich in parietal and occipital interhemispheric fibers ref [11]. Subsequent research confirmed these findings across diverse cohorts, including both high-functioning and intellectually disabled individuals, indicating that callosal reductions are not confined to a specific cognitive subgroup ref [74]. A study by Piven et al. demonstrated that after controlling for total brain volume, the body and posterior CC regions were significantly smaller in autistic individuals compared to matched controls ref [67]. Further regional analyses using high-resolution morphometry identified that normocephalic individuals with ASD exhibit specific reductions in the genu and midbody, while macrocephalic ASD individuals show overall larger CC size driven by midbody expansion, suggesting distinct neuroanatomical subtypes ref [63].

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) has extended these findings by revealing reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) within and near the CC in ASD, indicating compromised white matter microstructural integrity that persists into adulthood ref [62]. These microstructural alterations correlate with impaired interhemispheric communication and are thought to underlie the atypical functional connectivity observed in ASD. Notably, while some studies report early white matter overgrowth in young children with ASD, this is followed by a trajectory of reduced CC volume and integrity by adolescence and adulthood, pointing to a dynamic, non-linear developmental path ref [62]. Collectively, these structural anomalies support the hypothesis that disrupted interhemispheric connectivity is a core neurobiological feature of ASD, contributing to deficits in social cognition, sensory integration, and motor coordination.

subsections.section_title: Supplementary Materials
subsections.subsection_title: ADHD and Corpus Callosum Structure/Function
subsections.content:
Structural abnormalities of the corpus callosum (CC) are consistently reported in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), particularly in posterior regions. Morphometric MRI analyses reveal significantly reduced splenial area in ADHD populations, with this finding replicated across multiple studies and confirmed in meta-analytic reviews ref [52]. The splenium, which connects occipital and parietal cortices, is implicated in visuospatial attention and interhemispheric transfer of sensory information, potentially explaining sustained attention deficits characteristic of ADHD ref [9]. Some studies also report smaller rostral body volumes in males with ADHD, suggesting subtype- and sex-specific morphological patterns ref [52].

Beyond gross morphology, functional impairments in transcallosal communication are evident in ADHD. Electrophysiological studies using event-related potentials demonstrate altered interhemispheric transfer times, with distinct patterns observed between inattentive and combined subtypes—slower right-to-left transfer in the inattentive subtype and faster left-to-right transfer in the combined subtype ref [7]. Transcranial magnetic stimulation further reveals prolonged ipsilateral silent period (iSP) latencies and reduced iSP duration in children with ADHD, indicating compromised transcallosal motor inhibition, possibly due to defective myelination or imbalanced cortical excitation-inhibition ref [11]. These findings suggest that CC dysfunction in ADHD involves both structural underdevelopment and impaired functional integration between hemispheres.

While some studies report no differences in CC shape or anterior regions ref [9], the convergence of evidence from structural MRI, DTI, and neurophysiological methods supports a role for posterior callosal deficits in the neurobiology of ADHD. Longitudinal data on whether these abnormalities persist into adulthood remain limited, and the influence of comorbidities or medication, such as methylphenidate, on callosal integrity warrants further investigation ref [8].
